content:
These guys make more money than any other DoorDash drivers… here’s why…

I’m only talking about this as a metaphor, so hang with me.

The DoorDash marketplace is the epitome of a market that you shouldn’t be able to hack.

Customer orders, if you’re nearby you get that order.

But these guys are smart.

It’s 10am, they are outside a bakery that does >$55M a year. Drivers are tipped based on a % of the order. So if someone orders croissants for an office, that could be a nice tip. And since it’s reliable, they camp out here.

But for this to work, they have to NOT be anywhere else. They made a choice.

In the digital world, sadly we think we can be everywhere all at once.

Everything to everyone. 

We tell our customers “we are the very best at AI implementation” but that sentence makes no sense. So buyers don’t believe you.

It’s much easier to convince someone, “we are the best at helping plastics companies build Ai workflows from their ERP to their customers’ systems to track order delivery” or whatever.

You have no competition if you do that, or at least only two other guys who are in that lane.

So the customer knows you understand them.

If your message is “I can deliver you any item as fast as possible from anywhere in the city.” buyers know you’re full of it.

But, “I’m outside of Tartine right now and they have 25 croissants left and I’m only 15 minutes away from 4th and Market.” 

Well suddenly you become credible!

What’s a message, even that is fictional because you don’t yet have the data, that NONE of your competitors can send?

Work backwards from there.

content:
There are two newish Claude Code features I think will allow you to advance into the future before everyone else…

To be clear, I have just started my thinking around this.

But every once and awhile, apart from models, there’s a MUCH better WAY to work.

I think one way, in my line of work, to think about this better way to work is in these buckets.

1. What objective truth do I seek?
2. What is the greatest thing I can imagine?
3. If I did it by hand, and I had unlimited time, what would I do?

These are the macro questions I always ask myself and the two features I’m sorta obsessed with learning right now are goals and loops.

A loop is a run that keeps checking on things (based on spend, time, or even turns) and you get to like run a prompt again at certain intervals.

A goal is basically “continually do this until Haiku says you met the goal.”

The problem here is division. You need goals that a person could achieve (is this a penny and how sure are you) v.s. (is this information true, I don’t know how you’d know but run until you do.)

The thing is that you need to basically divide up tasks into goals that are achievable:

1. Goal: Do more than 2 sources say that X person works at Y company (yes or no). Loop: validate the work after 30 minutes and determine if the goal needs better information or kill it if it’s not making progress and you have exhausted all ideas.

2. Can you find a time on this source (yes,no). Loop, monitor that the sources dates seem plausible and double check their work, end if you aren’t seeing additional progress, if you find good information improve the instructions to the goal to look for those time sources in the most efffective ways.

If you can mentally divide your work into achievable goals, and a loop that improves based on the learning and stops when it isn’t making progress… you suddenly can dramatically improve your outcomes without much intervention.

This is why you should talk to the models and ask them to help divide up your task in thoughtful loops and useful goals and a loop should monitor the goal subagents to see if the extra time and spend is producing measurable results. Or if it should be stopped and a human should be involved again.

I’m just starting to open up my thinking about how these live in GTM workflows (validating data for sure). But it’s starting to change how I think about using Claude Code and Codex.

We need to stop being obsessed with tools, it has to stop.

Don’t get me wrong I love a good foundational model price cut, Fable was killing my budget.

And, don’t get me wrong, having an agent go fill out return paperwork is a blessing.

But, for the fundamental stuff GTM Engineers do… it hasn’t seemed to change anything for.

The creativity of the output
The quality of the output
The speed of quality output
The amount of quality outcomes
Our ability to ship quality outcomes to market

We still miss what matters most, and we have since before GPT-3.5. That is, what matters to our customers.

Sometimes I feel like we need to drop all this AI and just sit down with 5 customers and ask…

Be straight, buying software is hard, and current states are sticky. When it comes down to it, why did you really buy?

What did you consider before you bought?

What would have happened if you had not bought?

What is your primary ambition or worry in your job? (Which they pick matters).

If you were me, and had to sell to other buyers like you, what’s the one most important truth you learned about product that mattered much more than anyone else.

What do you know or believe about our product that you think we don’t or aren’t properly valuing.

I know hiding behind an LLM is fun (I love using it), but honestly figuring out what to ship, doing it with near-0 mid-quality people, or with only a handful of high duality people, and shipping often… that’s what matters most.

So go ahead, adopt the latest AI craze, but I bet that it won’t change anything about the value you’re able to deliver to the market.

I bet it will be super fun, and I bet that the opportunity cost to play with it for days will be astronomically high and you’ll likely be completely blinded to the fact that, still, today, in october of 2026… we still won’t know what to build, because we have the voice of agents in our heads, not the voice of our customers.

Or just let AI drive you around in circles forever, your choice.

The world’s greatest startup accelerator is betting on AI doing all of outbound, and it’s so ridiculous.

This problem is an insidious one, because the thesis SOUNDS GOOD. Just research someone until the cows come home, and once they come home, just talk about all the cheese you’re going to make with them.

I will say it loud and clear, hacking attention is not our problem.

1. The hacks stop working￼
2. You create downstream problems making the sales calls MUCH harder 
3. You can’t scale anything because this relies on putting more people top of the funnel. And, see problem 1.

So instead of just throwing mud, I’m going to outline how you should think about this problem:

1. First identify if there is some niche where a specific type of customer gets WAY more value. 
2. Understand the shape of that value that you can provide.
3. Use AI to pull and SEGMENT the world of your TAM
4. Tell them your hypothesis about what you know that they don’t, that they clamor to know, and what can benefit them.

There’s a thousand ways to do this, here’s an example of value at scale I posted on the only Substack I contribute to these days, my own (On The Edge)

https://lnkd.in/gP2ufR6s

But we must first seek to understand 1 customer segment 10x better than anyone in the market and be able to speak to them like a peer.

This is why these GTM tools are selling off and don’t have venture outcomes…. because this work involves understanding, creativity, and automation.

I have rarely seen any GTM team that has these qualities in their team. And, until we fix that, sales tools will continue to be snakeoil to those who will buy them because they have the same problem you do, which is they haven’t picked a customer with a problem that is in dire need, but the worst part about it is that they are clueless about it and you buy because you’re desperate… creating worse overall value for the market.

A great GTM engineer’s job is to produce art, but like a scientist. Here’s how I see it:

Go-to-market engineering is not rev ops, it’s not sales, it’s not marketing, it’s something new.

To do it well you need to begin with principles:

1. You must understand your customer’s role, how it fits in their org, and how central your product is to their purpose in the org.
2. You must know their universe of choices in your product category.
3. You must know what motivates your customer, why they do their job.

People skip these steps, which means they are wayfinding without a compass.

Once you have those, your artistic job begins:

Your singular role as an artist is to figure out the art your customers appreciate, this is often just a message that speaks to them using your compass and the principles of influence.

Components of a good messaging strategy include:

1. What information do they prize?
2. Who do they trust?
3. What brings them joy (not used often)?
4. What keeps them up at night?

Only then can you do the engineering part of your job, which is pretty simple. It’s just:

“How do you come up with hypotheses for which segments and run them through different channels, eliminating what doesn’t work and then scaling the tests that do.”

People often begin here, but those people have no guidance, no human understanding. Claude will replace those people.

But ChatGPT won’t easily replace the artist, because they have a process to consistently understand the customer and adapt as they change. That’s a moat AGI I don’t think will ever close, because it’s deeply human and what moves us isn’t word prediction, it’s emotional understanding.

I wanted to continue the linkedin trend of quoting yourself, and then posting the quote and agreeing with yourself. I know you’re supposed to screenshot your tweet, but this is all I got.

Anywho, I think the whole value of a brand new technology is abstraction. And knowing the primitives DOES help you, but it becomes less valuable overtime.

Every big invention made an old skill invisible.

Here's the timeline:

1712 — To build a steam engine, you had to know metal and heat.

1882 — To make electricity work, you had to know wires and grids.

1908 — You just flipped a switch. The lights came on.

1945 — To run a computer, you had to know tubes, wires, and 1s and 0s.

1957 — You stopped writing machine code. You wrote FORTRAN.

1972 — You stopped thinking about hardware. You wrote C.

1984 — You stopped typing commands. You clicked a mouse.

1993 — You stopped learning networks. You opened a web browser.

1998 — You stopped memorizing websites. You just Googled it.

2006 — You stopped running servers. You used the cloud.

2007 — You stopped needing a computer. You tapped a phone.

2010s — You stopped managing memory. You wrote Python.

2022 — You stopped writing code for lots of tasks. You asked ChatGPT.

2025 — You describe it in plain English. Claude Code builds it.

Every jump made the old skill unnecessary if you wanted to accomplish a derivative outcome from the tool.

AI amplifies your own lack of context, which is why so many AI projects fail--here's how I think about success -> failure with AI projects.

There's a spectrum with AI projects
1. Automate {{human job}}
2. Automate {{human task}}
3. Solve {{hard semi-known problem}} technically 

Let's talk about each of these...

1. I think only a few individuals have tried to actually do this, mostly for content (OpenClaw). But entire businesses have been built on this, most have troubles if they pick a job that AI + software is not actually great at replacing. Most jobs have too much human in them.

2. This is where most investment is, but the single biggest problem is when context is unstated, unknown, or too much human judgement is involved. Honestly, a lot of my campaigns have fallen into this trap. Because the model makes too many choices that aren't your choices. There is usually a very small amount of logical cohesion here.

3. This is where AI shines. Where basically, with ENOUGH RAW work a thing can be done. Think about like reading through tons of documents, doing competitor technology sniffing, correlating a bunch of data that was basically impossible before.

The beauty with number 3 is that:
1. You can OBSERVE the outcome at the ROW level and it's deterministic.
2. You can ask questions you never could have before from multiple data sets
3. This requires imagination, but not trust, and the model can do unique discovery.

I think so many people are getting way more tied up in projects like number 2, where you haven't narrowed down the task, where there are too many human choices, and where the outputs are so hard to evaluate... you're just not sure where to go.

I think it's best to let the models mix and match data, to find unique correlations, to do a bunch of discovery---but only for DETERMINISTIC problems, not human tasks.

The key to all AI initiatives is to limit the scope of the problem to be both constrained and very imaginative + easily know what great looks like at the row level.

This is the magic of AI, but picking WHAT to do is 90% of the challenge and the other 10% is the how. And the how is vastly getting better. But that 90%, that's not changing at all.

===============
“{{generic summarized fact about me that sounds like a robot wrote it}}”

Not to put too fine of a point on this, but if you manually inspect your list and you find someone that literally sells a variant of what you do, then your list sucks. And if your list sucks, your message has no chance.

You can’t write your way out of a targeting problem, but you can target your way out of a pipeline problem.

The real question is, do you REALLY know who should and shouldn’t buy and why? 

Answer that question first and the targeting and messaging will be easy, because it’s just weeding out the bad prospects and describing to the good ones why they should receive your message.

HOT TAKE: SDRs deserve the heated replies they get from prospects.

Each week you see SDRs taking screenshots of replies from buyers that are like… “this person told me to jump off a cliff”

The invariable response looks like this:
1. Shouldn’t they know how sales works
2. We don’t want to work with people like that
3. Yah what a jerk, he must be disturbed

But this totally misses the point because 100% of the empathy is deployed to THE SELLER.

But sales isn’t about feeling sorry for ourselves, it’s not about us, it’s about the buyer.

If we are triggering our buyers to respond like that, don’t WE have the responsibility to not send messages that trigger such replies?

So here are some ideas to not get yelled at:

1. Copy and paste all your transcripts into Claude and ask, “what secrets did buyers share that are counterintuitive and give me their names and titles, here’s a spreadsheet of the calls I have uploaded to correlate them. Now you can share SECRETS of their peers.

2. Go figure out if they are hiring for roles, and see if you know someone and begin with a few recommendations for people in your network (or at your company) that would be good fits.

3. Go figure out your internal company problems and seek out vendors and explain what’s going on internally to VPs of Sales at companies who could help.

4. Go figure out if they are going to a conference and scraoe the attendees list or exhibitor list for them.

5. Want to be BALLER, go figure out who has spoke recently at conferences and send the speakers customized gifts on behalf of the conference. The go to the conference folks and share with them what you did and let them take credit.

6. Do the play above, but for recent case studies. Here’s your intro email “Jordan, I read your case study with bob at frolic construction. I did some research on bob and he loves racing so I’d like to send him a day at the track, paid for by my company, but on your behalf to thank him for his case study. His address is X from what I can tell. You want me to add a custom handwritten note? I have a budget to spend anyways, and might as well do something nice for you instead of cold pitch.”

People are just TIRED of TAKING and SAMENESS.

If you just don’t take, and try to give, and you’re like 15% weirder than everyone else… novelty plus kindness WILDLY pays off.

The only reason I haven’t had to do outbound for my business in a long time is I try to put this type of energy out into the universe.

It pays back at such a dividend that I never need to force my business to grow, it grows on its own, even when my business model is designed for 100% churn.

So stop posting mean replies, earn amazing replies, and recognize that the locus of control is on you.

You’re the only one that can plant the seeds to change your circumstance. To get upset with our buyers is to invite laziness into your thoughts, to invite a mindset of failure.

Go make exceptional experiences for your buyers and you’ll want for nothing.

content:
If you don’t enjoy your job, and you’re reading this, there IS a WAY out.

This is my favorite book, the Wisdom of Insecurity by Alan Watts.

I want to be tactical, though, you can create your own luck. You can navigate out of your situation.

But to do so requires some advice from the Shawshank Redemption:

Pressure Over Time

Optionality is built in years and months, not days and weeks.

The best optionality is built by becoming an expert, and it’s usually by combining two things (in my case, customer empathy and data w/ AI). I’m the best in the world ONLY when you mix those three things. This is a Ben Horowitz concept, and it’s beautiful.

But the way in which you can get everything that you wanted is to find out what you enjoy doing, and just begin.

Begin by working on it, talking to people about it, building little prototypes, working for people or companies for free to learn it. 

When you do that, you subtly convince the other people that love what you love that you’re in it for passion. 

This is the single thing that people want to hire for, a hunger for the work itself. For its own sake.

Weather it’s gardening, or dental hygiene, or making hats, or ice skating… I promise you there are others out there that feel the way you feel.

Then, once you know them, and once they know your only agenda is to find joy in what you do… they FIND ways to help you. Because they see the joy, they likely feel the joy, and they want other people to feel the joy.

The people I completely avoid building relationships with are those that are money driven, not because it’s bad (I love money), but just because it’s the outcome they seek not the process they love.

That only gets you so far, because you lose your purpose when you make enough money. All that money ever got me, besides freedom from 9-5, is a ridiculously over priced coffee grinder. 

Start working on the side, finding your community, doing the things you feel drawn to… and when you do, you’ll draw in others.

And one day you’ll wake up, and you’ll have so much optionality you won’t know how to chose.

That’s when you really become free, when you get to define your days around your joy, not your job.

Invest daily now, and I promise it will compound over enough time.

I have stopped an experiment that gave people a ton of value before a sale, and here's why...

So it's VERY fast for me to build a PVP or PQS list, like 30 mins -> 1 hr. 

Now this list isn't like ALWAYS production ready, but it's usually good enough for a test. So I tried just giving these things to prospects after a first call, in addition to my standard vibe coded proposal.

This was A TERRIBLE idea and probably lost me over $120k, and here's why...

People actually don't want to buy results... and hear me out.

Results are ephemeral, this is why every lead generation agency is always on the razor's edge. When I ran a lead gen agency, people said, "sure this year I made $2M in closed/won deals and paid you $120k, BUT WHAT HAVE YOU DONE FOR ME THIS MONTH."

This isn't true with Google or Facebook, because they have a monopoly and you have no choice, so they can enforce rules (you pay for clicks).

People would take these lists, sometimes even execute on them, and then I suspect they didn't get good results and said, "THAT GUY SUCKS!"

I just feel so much apathy… 

There’s an insidious thing about AI, maybe the most dehumanizing part…

That it makes me question how genuine people are based on the quality of their writing. 

As if they write like AI, I tend to round down and think even less of the message. Like somehow bad message written by a computer is even worse.

I hate questioning if the person sucks at messaging or they suck at using AI, because it’s kinda a question of what is genuine.

Let’s break this message down:

Pros:
1. It talks about me and my post.
2. It connects my value prop with what I do.
3. It mostly feels personalized, like it was written for me.

Cons:
1. It’s so so long.
2. It uses the word “interesting” which is the least interesting word in existence.
3. It says a lot without communicating anything specifically, classic AI sign.
4. It’s asking for 15 mins (a terrible amount of time, like it’s 30 or bust for me)
5. It talks about networking — No busy executive wants to network. They want to solve problems.
6. It’s just so generic as to make me feel the call will be an utter waste of time as there’s no SYNTHESIS of information.

Now contrast tho next message, which is about a specific piece of content, uses the word ingenious, is not asking me for time, and feels authentic to me.

Here’s an exercise, just write yourself a cold message YOU would happily respond to…

Here’s mine…

“Jordan, I’m 42 minutes into your video on systems of actions, systems of record, and systems of information and it’s been 3 months, what’s changed in how you’re building systems of information?”

Or here’s another one,

“Jordan I’ve heard from some friends that you do $3k campaign builds live for people in 2 hours? Can I buy that.”

Or this one,

“Jordan, I run a startup backed by a16z that builds an AI SDR for just logistics companies and we’re building it based on 17 public data sets and we’d like to make you an advisor.”

Or this one,

“Jordan I am pretty sure you’re wrong about Claude Code’s agent mode replacing Claygent—I could only get it to work for like 200 rows. What’s your secret?”

Notice that all of these messages carry specificity, they embed my point of view (the AI SDR one I would take that call because they have talked about HOW they are doing it and made choices that makes it unique).

In the other case, they want to pay me, BANGER!

In the first case they have focused 100% on my ideas, which makes me believe they literally care about the ideas. Which I love talking about of course!

And the last message is actually true, I was wrong!

There’s a thing in blockchain called proof of work, Sam McKenna says it as show me you know me, but I don’t think either of these are useful anymore.

As there are more demands on my time, I dont want you to prove you have read my things, I want you to demonstrate that you have synthesized them, disagree with them, have a damn opinion.

And in a world of AI, the winners will be those who can not just write well, but think well.

Thing 2:

Just ask a customer about their research, their options, what mattered to them, why, what they didn’t consider. Inhabit their worldview.

You can’t own framing the problem if you’re clueless about their world, and you can’t know where you best fit in if you don’t know where other tools best you.

The art comes in talking about HOW you do what you do NOT outcomes. You need to have a POV that makes what you do compelling.

Once you do that, all you do is:
1. Find out who is in that situation with data
2. Explain your read problem space to them
3. Help them buy the right tool for them (even if it’s not yours)
